stimuli.description: Simulated office environments with three conditions: no window (blue panels), window view of nature (trees, blue sky), and window with shutters (daylight infiltration without view).

tables.description: Descriptive statistics (mean and standard deviation) for positive affect (PA), negative affect (NA), simple reaction time task (SRTT), 2-back discrimination score (2-back DS), and 2-back reaction time (2-back RT) across no-window, daylight, and nature-view conditions.

limitations: The obviousness of the experimental manipulation and within-participants design could create a potential for expectation and social desirability bias.
The counterbalancing of conditions minimized, but did not completely rule out, order effects.
The use of blue shutters and panels to minimize visual differences might have also minimized the contrast to the biophilic condition.
The panels in the windowless condition could have been perceived as a 'blocked-window' rather than a 'no-window' condition.
The use of self-reported measures of affect may create limitations to the internal validity of the study due to social desirability bias.
VR simulations are artificially created and do not include additional sensory information (e.g., temperature).
Participants were not cognitively fatigued, which may have diminished any potential restorative effect on attentional function.
A longer exposure duration could have increased effects of the environment on attentional functions.
The amount of nature offered in the current experiment was not enough to elicit 'fascination' or 'widening of attention' to trigger enhanced cognitive flexibility.
